# Metasploit Framework

An exploitation framework: a catalogued library of exploit modules, payloads, encoders and auxiliary
tools behind a common console (`msfconsole`). Appears in lab 12 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]], against a deliberately vulnerable Metasploitable VM.

**This page describes the tool's structure and what the lab attempted. It contains no module names in
use, no payload, no exploitation procedure and no privilege-escalation steps.** See the redaction note
on [[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]].

## The structure worth knowing

The framework's design is the transferable part, because it is a clean separation of concerns:

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **Exploit module** | the technique that gains code execution against a specific flaw |
| **Payload** | what runs afterwards — the two are chosen independently |
| **Encoder** | reshapes a payload to survive transport constraints or naive filtering |
| **Auxiliary** | scanning, fingerprinting and enumeration that does not exploit |
| **Post** | modules that run once access exists |

Decoupling exploit from payload is why one framework covers so much ground: *n* exploits and *m*
payloads give *n × m* combinations without either side knowing about the other. It also explains the
defensive posture — detecting the payload family is often easier and more durable than detecting each
individual exploit.

## Where it sits in the chain

Lab 12 runs the standard sequence: enumerate with [[nmap]], identify service versions, look up known
vulnerabilities for those exact versions, then search the framework's catalogue for a matching module.
That is the value proposition — the framework is a **searchable index** from "this version is running"
to "this is known to be exploitable", which is what turns a version string from trivia into a finding.
See [[network-reconnaissance]].

## What actually happened in the lab

The chain did not complete. The report records the port scan failing to return a version for a service
that was demonstrably running, an unexpected port state, and the final step producing a connection
that yielded nothing usable — the report's own words are that the target directory came back empty.
The privilege-escalation exercise that followed is not described here at all.

**TODO:** whether these were tooling problems, environment problems, or a conceptual gap is not
diagnosed anywhere in the repository, and whether the exercise was retried is unrecorded.
`confidence: low` on lab 12's completion; `confidence: medium` on this page overall, since the
framework's role is documented in the README and its structure is not repo-specific.

That an exploitation lab is the *least* complete in a fourteen-lab set is itself a finding —
exploitation against a prepared target is fragile, version-sensitive and unforgiving of small
environment differences, in a way that the measurement labs are not.

## Scope

Coursework, 2022, against Metasploitable and other deliberately vulnerable images provided for the
purpose. The repository states that nothing was run against a system without authorisation and that
none of it is written as an operational guide; this wiki keeps to the same boundary and narrows it.
